4: Purpose: decide whether THAT space works and how many pieces a day the equipment you're buying can handle.
6: 1. "Settings" sheet: start here. Shift hours, shifts per day, pieces you want to turn out, square footage, power and fuel type of the ovens. Everything else in the workbook recalculates from here; there isn't a single number hidden inside a formula.
7: 2. "Zones and Square Feet" sheet: split the square feet among the seven zones and number the one-way flow route from 1 to 7. The sheet tells you whether the split matches the declared square footage, what share of the space is production kitchen and whether the route has a crossing.
8: 3. "Capacity by Equipment" sheet: one row per machine. Say whether you have it, how much fits in a cycle, how many pieces come out of that amount, how many minutes the cycle lasts and what share of your assortment goes through it. The sheet returns the pieces per day THAT machine allows the whole production kitchen.
9: 4. "Bottleneck" sheet: the result. Which machine is in charge, how many pieces a day the whole kitchen can handle, how much cushion you have over a normal day and what happens in each of the six peaks of the year. This is where you see whether Three Kings Day fits in the production kitchen you're buying.
10: 5. "Site Visit Checklist" sheet: print it and take it to every visit. Eighteen checks, eight of them deal-breakers. A single "No" on a deal-breaker item and the verdict is RULE OUT: it's not pessimism, it's that the defect can't be fixed with reasonable money.

12: What to know before you start
13: THIS WORKBOOK DECIDES A PURCHASE, NOT A WORK WEEK. Day-to-day production -what gets made on Tuesday and how much- belongs with your daily task checklists. Here we only answer how many pieces a day the equipment you're about to pay for allows, the question you can't answer after you've bought.
14: THE SHARE OF THE ASSORTMENT IS THE COLUMN MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN. A blast chiller that 40% of what you make goes through, and that chills 192 pieces a day, doesn't limit your kitchen to 192 pieces: it limits it to 480. Without that column, any capacity calculation comes out wrong, and always on the low side.
15: PEAKS AREN'T SOLVED WITH OVERTIME. Three Kings Day multiplies a normal day's production by six. No team absorbs that: you absorb it with scheduled freezing, shelf-stable product made ahead and custom orders closed in advance. The peak calendar and what to do in each one belong in your annual task calendar and daily task checklists; the dollars of each campaign are in seasonal-peaks-planner.xlsx.
16: THE HOOD IS DECIDED BY TYPE, NOT BY ONE NUMBER. In the US the hood type follows the appliance, its listing and the mechanical code your jurisdiction has adopted (IMC 507): Type I with grease duct and fire suppression where appliances give off grease or smoke, Type II for heat and steam, and none for a single light-duty electric oven or an appliance listed to UL 710B. Get the answer in writing from the building or mechanical department. The airflow on the "Settings" sheet is a sizing rule of thumb, not a legal threshold.
17: PRICES AND LEAD TIMES AREN'T HERE. What each machine costs and how many weeks it takes to arrive are in startup-cost-calculator.xlsx and equipment-and-suppliers-checklist.xlsx. This workbook only looks at what the machines produce.

54: La Clara works one early-morning shift. A second shift is the cheapest lever there is for raising capacity, and the most expensive one in labor.
55: Productive hours as a share of the workday

61: Shift hours × shifts × productive hours × 60. This is where each piece of equipment's cycles per day come from.
64: 6 days a week × 52 weeks = 312, minus 12 closing days for a vacation in August = 300. Holidays are NOT subtracted: you choose your own days and hours (check your lease and local rules).
66: 312 days open minus 12 closing days for vacation.

248: The six peaks of the year
253: Pieces per day the whole kitchen allows
257: Star product units per day during the campaign
263: The peak that decides the year. The campaign units are those of the FIVE best-selling days: 160 a day, 800 in total, 47% of the roscas the menu mix assigns to the year (1.2% of the pieces). The rest sell in the week before, outside the campaign window, which is why they aren't in this row. In the US the rosca shares its season with the king cake (Epiphany to Mardi Gras), and searches average about 90,500 a month for "rosca de reyes" and 110,000 for "king cake" (DataForSEO, October 2026): scale references, never price or market share. A cream-filled rosca carries the 41 °F cold-holding limit (Food Code 3-501.16) and date marking (3-501.17) on the biggest production day: that limits production as much as the oven does.
267: Two-day, high-ticket campaign, not volume: you win with boxes and presentation, not with more oven. The special production for this date is heart-shaped cakes, bonbons and macarons.
269: Día de las Madres (May 10) and US Mother's Day (2nd Sunday of May)
271: One operating date for Día de las Madres (May 10) and US Mother's Day (2nd Sunday of May): a personalized cake, made to order. What matters to this guide is the load on the production kitchen, not the calendar.
275: Eight days in a row of extra production, more exhausting than the five of Three Kings Day even though the peak is smaller. Torrijas and Easter cakes (monas) at once: one needs a fryer and cold, the other an oven and chocolate. That's 230 torrijas a day and 1,840 over the campaign: 99% of the torrijas the menu mix assigns to the year, because they aren't made outside Holy Week.
279: It's not a peak, it's a two-month PLATEAU, which is why you carry it with staff and not with overtime. Everything is by custom order: deposit, delivery calendar and cancellation risk (chapter 16).
280: All Saints' Day and Día de los Muertos
283: Three days with three items that are only made now: buñuelos, huesos de santo and panellets. The buñuelos are cream-filled (41 °F or below, and date-marked if held) and the other two are shelf-stable at room temperature: that's why buñuelos are made the same day and huesos de santo can be made ahead. That food-safety detail IS the campaign planning. It's 470 buñuelos a day and 1,410 over the three days: 99% of the buñuelos the menu mix assigns to the year, because they aren't made outside this date.
289: One peak is more than the kitchen can take
290: Several peaks are more than the kitchen can take
291: A peak that doesn't fit in the production kitchen is NOT a reason to buy more machine: buying for Three Kings Day means having money sitting idle the other 299 days. What you do is get ahead on production (scheduled freezing with a blast chiller, not a chest freezer), load the campaign onto shelf-stable items that can be made days ahead, and close orders with a date. Each campaign's dollars are in seasonal-peaks-planner.xlsx; its dates and task list belong in your annual task calendar.
292: The column "star product units per day during the campaign" is here as a contrast, not a calculation: it's the units of the product that defines the peak. The 420 roscas a day on Three Kings Day versus zero on a normal day are the reason this sheet exists.
294: Print it and take it to every visit. A single "No" on a deal-breaker item and the verdict is RULE OUT.
304: There's a route for the hood's own duct up to the roof
305: Go up on the roof with the landlord and look at where the duct would run; it can't tie into the restroom or front-of-house exhaust. Get it in writing before you sign.
312: Industry rule of thumb, NOT a verified code: the duct usually has to reach the roof, and how far above it and how far from air intakes and property lines is set by your adopted mechanical code and NFPA 96: ask the building department. It's the item that rules out the most spaces and the one to settle BEFORE you sign, not after.
313: The hood type the space has (or can take) matches your ovens
314: Type I with fire suppression for deck ovens, Type II for enclosed electric convection: get the answer in writing from the building or mechanical department. Ask for the mechanical plans or open the dropped ceiling to see what's there.
315: Hood type follows the appliance, its listing and your jurisdiction's adopted mechanical code (IMC 507): Type I with grease duct and fire suppression where appliances give off grease or smoke, Type II for heat and steam, and none for a single light-duty electric oven or an appliance listed to UL 710B. Don't read those exceptions as yours: a Type II where your ovens need a Type I means a new hood, duct and fire suppression system to budget.
316: The available exhaust airflow covers what your ovens need
317: Measure it, or ask for the spec sheet of the existing exhaust fan. The threshold is calculated on the "Settings" sheet from your oven power and your fuel type.
318: Sizing rule of thumb: 23.5 CFM per kW for electric equipment and 29.4 for gas. If the space falls short, the cost of replacing the exhaust fan goes into startup-cost-calculator.xlsx.
319: The electrical service available covers what you're going to install
320: Ask for the service size (amps, voltage, single- or three-phase) and ask the utility what capacity the building's service can deliver.
321: Raising the available power of a service can cost more than the whole build-out and depends on the utility, not on your budget.
322: Zoning allows a bakery with on-site production at that address
323: Ask the planning or zoning department, in writing and for that specific address, not over the phone. Ask whether they issue a zoning verification letter.
324: A space that's a store today doesn't automatically allow a production kitchen: it's food production, with exhaust and early-morning hours.
325: The landlord and the center's CC&Rs or rules allow the use, the hood and the roof penetration
326: Get the landlord's written approval and read the CC&Rs or the center or association rules. A restaurant next door isn't proof enough.
327: A recorded restriction or a center rule binds you even if the city gives you the permit, and the duct usually crosses a common area or the roof.
328: The clear ceiling height reaches the height you've set
329: Laser measure from the finished floor to the underside of the structure, at the lowest point, not the highest.
330: With hood, duct and dropped ceiling, every inch counts. Measure where the oven goes.
331: The usable floor area covers the square feet you've allotted by zone
332: Real usable area, not counting walls or shafts. Compare it with the total on the "Zones and Square Feet" sheet.
333: A listing's square footage is usually gross. The one that matters is usable, and about 108 sq ft can easily vanish between the two.
334: The production kitchen can be closed off so customers can't get in
335: Draw the seven zones on the floor plan before you sign. If they don't fit with the door where it is, they don't fit.
336: The production kitchen is a prep area off-limits to customers. It's not a design recommendation: it's what separates a production kitchen from a kitchen on display.
337: The seven zones fit with a one-way flow and no crossings
338: Check the route on the "Zones and Square Feet" sheet: ingredients, production kitchen, finished goods, counter.
339: Fitting the square feet doesn't mean fitting the route. A production kitchen where the trash goes out the way the flour comes in won't pass plan review.
340: There's hot and cold water and a drain where the equipment goes
341: Find the existing drains. Moving a drain means cutting up the slab across the whole space.
342: A steam oven, the blast chiller and the sinks need a drain at their spot, not at the far end of the space.
343: Floors and walls can take a smooth, durable, easily cleanable finish, with coved floor-wall junctions
344: Look at the real condition: cracked tile, bare drywall, raw concrete. A kitchen finish is construction, not paint.
345: Smooth, durable, easily cleanable surfaces (Food Code 6-201.11), coved floor-wall junctions (6-201.13) and a hand sink where people work (5-203.11). In Texas, walls and ceilings in prep areas have to be light in color (25 TAC §228.171). It isn't an extra: it's a requirement.
346: There's room for a staff restroom and changing area
347: Count the square feet and find where the drain stacks are; your local plumbing code sets how many restrooms you need. A new restroom with no stack nearby is a big job.
348: Staff need their own restroom and locker space; customers have theirs. The 118 sq ft on the zones sheet (restrooms and lockers) already account for it.
349: Deliveries can come in without crossing the customer area
350: Go at the hour you'd take deliveries, not at noon. Check for a loading zone or a back door, and whether the building allows it.
351: Flour comes in sacks, every day. If it comes in through the front door, it comes past the customer every morning.
352: Trash goes out without opening into the production kitchen
353: Find the trash room or enclosure and its door. It has to be closed, with labeled bins.
354: The trash area can't open into the production kitchen. It's one of the few floor-plan defects with no cheap fix.
355: The space is accessible or can be made accessible
356: Measure the entry step and the door width. A step at the entrance may be the landlord's or the city's call, not yours.
357: Customers have to be able to get in and be served. The standard for a sales counter is a stretch no higher than 36 inches (ADA Standards 904.4.1). Who pays for entrance changes (you, the landlord or the city) depends on the lease and local rules: ask before you sign.
358: Verified October 2026 · ADA Standards for Accessible Design, §904.4.1 (sales and service counters) · https://www.access-board.gov/ada/chapter/ch09/
359: If you'll bake on gas, the gas service and piping can carry your ovens
360: Ask the gas utility for the meter size and pressure at the space, and ask the building department what permit and inspection new gas piping needs.
361: Gas ovens need the service, meter and piping sized for their load, and new piping needs its own permit and inspection. Get it in writing before you commit to gas; if you go electric, this item doesn't apply.
362: Gas piping permits and inspections vary by city and by utility, and no single national rule covers them: ask the building department and the gas utility.
363: The lease and what comes with the space are clear before you sign
364: Read the whole lease: use clause, permit contingency, CAM and NNN charges, personal guarantee, and who pays for the build-out (TI allowance).
365: Who pays for the build-out, how many years the lease runs and what happens to the improvements at the end are three numbers in startup-cost-calculator.xlsx, not three details.
378: The eight deal-breaker items aren't deal-breakers out of taste: they're the defects that can't be fixed with reasonable money, or that don't depend on you (the landlord, zoning, the electrical service, the roof). The rest make the build-out more expensive and have to go into startup-cost-calculator.xlsx as a line item, not rule out the space. And keep the checklist for the spaces you rule out: comparing three checklists is what shows you what you're accepting without realizing it.
